sources.title: V-JEPA 2.1: Unlocking Dense Features in Video Self-Supervised Learning

sectionsRead: 2.3.1–2.3.6 Dense loss, deep supervision, data, tokenizer, scaling and distillation (pp. 5–9)
3.5–3.10 Dense tasks, recognition, video QA, qualitative features and distilled models (pp. 15–23)
4 Related work and 5 Conclusion and Future work (pp. 20, 23–24)
Appendix A Pretraining and B Distillation (pp. 33–34)
omissions: Text extraction does not reconstruct figure images; inspect the retained PDF for figures and equation/table layout.
Separate supplemental material availability has not been fully verified.

All 11 supplied text chunks were read individually. The extraction limitation was addressed by visually inspecting PDF pages 1–24 and 33–37, including all numbered figures and tables; reference pages 25–32 were read as text.

Version scope: the supplied PDF is arXiv:2603.14482v3, stamped 11 June 2026, with a title-block date of June 12, 2026. The catalog submission date is March 15, 2026; earlier editions were not supplied or compared. The observed title and nine-author list match the catalog display. Its BibTeX uses Mahmoud Assran and Michael Rabbat where the observed credits say Mido Assran and Mike Rabbat; metadata preserves the observed credits.
The linked code, checkpoints and external datasets were not inspected. No training, evaluation or robot experiment was reproduced.

synopsis: V-JEPA 2.1 learns image/video patch features by predicting both hidden and visible representations at multiple encoder depths. This substantially improves dense vision while largely preserving global recognition; separate task heads and world models turn the features into anticipation and planning systems.

problem.text: Masked-only video representation learning can recognize actions while yielding fragmented patch features. The authors hypothesize that unsupervised visible tokens become global aggregators, leaving local geometry difficult to recover with a linear probe. The objective is to retain spatial detail, temporal consistency and global semantics together.

contributions.text: A distance-weighted visible-token loss complements masked prediction; deep supervision at four encoder levels repairs much of the accompanying recognition penalty.

Native image/video tokenizers, VisionMix163M, scaling to ViT-G and distillation form a transferable feature family; downstream evidence spans dense probes, forecasting and separately trained planners.

inputs: Unlabeled images and video clips during pretraining
Task-labeled examples for downstream probes; robot trajectories and visual goals for planning extensions
outputs: Dense spatiotemporal patch embeddings and predicted latent representations
Task-specific predictions or CEM-selected actions through separately trained downstream components

steps.name: Tokenize and mask
steps.detail: Use 16×16 image patches and 16×16×2 video tubelets, modality embeddings and 3D RoPE. The context encoder sees visible tokens; an EMA target encoder sees the complete input.

steps.name: Fuse encoder depths
steps.detail: Concatenate normalized representations from three intermediate blocks and the final block, then compress them with an MLP. Append positional mask tokens and predict representations at four levels. ViT-G uses blocks 12, 24, 36 and 48.

steps.name: Supervise both token sets
steps.detail: Apply L1 prediction error to masked tokens and weighted L1 error to visible tokens at each level. Context tokens nearer masked regions receive stronger weighting; gradients stop at the EMA targets.

training.text: VisionMix163M replaces ImageNet with 142M curated images and reweights video sources. Separate modality workers aggregate gradients, with global batches of 2,304 images and 128 clips. Pretraining lasts 135,000 steps at 256-pixel resolution and 16 video frames; 12,000 cooldown steps use 512-pixel images and 64-frame, 384-pixel videos.

The 24-block predictor has width 384. EMA is 0.99925, weight decay 0.04, and context coefficients are 0.5 for video and 0.7 for images. Distillation replaces the EMA target with a frozen ViT-G teacher, uses a new 12-block predictor and final-layer losses, and releases the averaged student. Low- and high-resolution teachers match the two training stages.

inference.text: Dense image tasks train linear probes on frozen final-layer features; VOS propagates initial masks through cosine-similarity neighbors. EK100 retains the frozen predictor to infer future-frame features and combines them with context features in an attentive classifier. These outputs describe future events rather than executing them.

Manipulation trains a separate frame-causal action-conditioned predictor on DROID with teacher-forcing and two-step rollout losses, then uses CEM model-predictive control. Navigation instead trains a conditional diffusion world model, predicts clean features with DDIM, and searches 480 candidate two-second trajectories in a three-degree-of-freedom action space.

equations.explanation: Equation (1): x is the masked view of clean input y; M indexes masked patches. E is the encoder, P the predictor, and Δ_y supplies positional mask tokens. θ̄ is the EMA of θ; sg stops gradients. Targets are learned features, not pixels.

Equations (2)–(3): C indexes visible context tokens. d_min measures the distance in blocks to the nearest masked token; λ sets the context-loss strength. The paper calls this term both L_context and L_ctx. Both losses apply at all four supervised depths.

results.setting: Cumulative ViT-L recipe; ADE20K linear and SSv2 attentive probes.
results.value: 22.2 / 72.8 → 33.8 / 62.5 with context loss → 38.6 / 72.1 with multi-level prediction.
results.comparison: Masked-only V-JEPA 2 is the starting row.
results.interpretation: Dense gains initially cost recognition accuracy. Use Table 1 values; prose gives 33.9 and 0.473 rather than 33.8 and 0.474 for context-only ADE20K/NYUv2.

results.setting: Ego4D STA v2 validation: 47,395 examples; train: 98,276. Frozen backbone plus trained detection/attention head.
results.comparison: V-JEPA 2 ViT-g: 6.02; same-protocol DINOv3 7B: 5.68; literature STAformer: 5.67.
results.interpretation: Requires correct noun/verb, box IoU >0.5 and contact time within 0.25 seconds; discounts four highest-scoring false positives. Input configuration conflicts remain.

results.setting: EK100 validation; 32 frames at 8 fps, 384×384; one-second anticipation.
results.interpretation: The larger model improves by 1.1 points over V-JEPA 2; the equal-size comparison does not improve.

results.setting: Zero-shot lab Franka Panda deployment; ten tasks per skill, CEM on one A100.
results.comparison: V-JEPA 2: 60% / 100% / 80%. Matched setting: 800 samples, 10 iterations, horizon 1, 3 seconds; longer: 300, 15, horizon 8, 14 seconds.
results.interpretation: Grasp improves by 10 percentage points with matched planning, or 20 points with changed planning. No confidence intervals are reported.

results.setting: Validation trajectories on Recon, Tartan Drive, Scand and Sacson; two-second plans.
results.value: ViT-G Tartan Drive: 5.687; average ATE: 2.990; time: 10.6 seconds.
results.interpretation: Approximately 9.7× faster, calculated from reported times; gains are not universal across datasets. This evaluates trajectory error, not closed-loop navigation success.

results.setting: Frozen final-layer single-image probes on NYUv2, KITTI and ADE20K; source benchmark evaluation.
results.interpretation: Strong improvement over V-JEPA 2; the small NYUv2 lead over DINOv3 has no uncertainty estimate and does not extend to KITTI or segmentation.

results.setting: DAVIS 2017 validation and a custom 20% holdout from YouTube-VOS training videos; nonparametric mask propagation.
results.interpretation: Improves correspondence quality but remains behind DINOv3. Table 14 instead lists 72.6 for high-resolution ViT-G YouTube-VOS.

results.setting: Frozen attentive probes, benchmark validation, multi-view video evaluation.
results.interpretation: Global capability is largely retained, with a Diving-48 regression. The SSv2 frame-count conflict prevents an unambiguous replication setting.

results.setting: Llama 3.1 8B alignment on filtered PerceptionLM; compare the two rows trained in this paper.
results.metric: Reported benchmark average / PerceptionTest validation accuracy
results.interpretation: Mixed transfer: TemporalBench and TOMATO decline. Older starred PerceptionTest results use the unavailable test server and are not directly comparable.
Distillation closes much of the gap; Table 11 gives teacher DAVIS 69.0, contrary to 67.0 in the distillation prose.

limitations.text: The authors attribute weaker cluttered-scene segmentation to limited exposure in VisionMix, but do not isolate that cause experimentally. They describe gripper timing and premature opening as remaining manipulation failure modes.

Sequential recipe gains combine objectives, data, capacity and resolution. Table 13 supports better final-layer features, not elimination of every multi-layer benefit. PCA displays are qualitative and their RGB permutation is selected for appearance.

Source inconsistencies remain: navigation Table 7 says finetuning while Section 3 describes frozen encoders; ATE is expanded differently in its caption and text. Table 14 also contains regressions despite the prose claiming universal resolution gains. These ambiguities are retained, not resolved by assumption.

reproduction.text: A full reproduction needs VisionMix source access, EMA/masking implementation, both training resolutions and task-specific probes. Appendix A specifies schedules but not pretraining GPU count, runtime or software versions. Its cooldown starts at 6e-4 after a 5.25e-4 plateau; Section 2.3.1 expresses context warmup in epochs without defining its conversion to steps.

Resolve Ego4D settings before reproducing 7.71: Section 3.1 uses eight frames over 0.5 seconds and four feature scales; Appendix C.4 selects 16 frames at 2 fps and lists five scales. SSv2 uses 16×2×3 in Table 9, but Appendix C.5 prints 64×2×3 while still saying 16-frame clips.

Reader-proposed checks: run a matched-budget factorial context-loss/deep-supervision ablation, then compare both encoders under identical short- and long-horizon CEM settings. The illustrated edition specifies controls and falsifiable outcomes; neither check was executed.

reasoning.text: The recorded foundational visual-encoder classification is supported. Base pretraining predicts latent visual tokens without action outputs. Manipulation and navigation add separate learned dynamics and search. Shared image/video encoding therefore does not establish a One Model world-action architecture or joint future/action prediction; the recorded architecture, paradigm and quadrant remain not applicable.

discussionQuestions: Would multi-level supervision recover recognition at fixed predictor capacity and pretraining budget?
Does the grasp improvement persist when both encoders receive identical horizon, search budget and repeated object configurations?

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title block and arXiv margin
evidence.detail: Exact observed title; nine authors: Lorenzo Mur-Labadia, Matthew Muckley, Amir Bar, Mido Assran, Koustuv Sinha, Mike Rabbat, Yann LeCun, Nicolas Ballas and Adrien Bardes. Affiliations: FAIR at Meta and Universidad de Zaragoza. Margin: v3, 11 Jun 2026; title date: June 12, 2026.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 3–4, Section 2.1 and Eq. (1)
evidence.detail: Predictor inputs are context and mask tokens; masked-only L1 targets come from a stop-gradient EMA encoder of the clean input.

evidence.location: PDF p. 4, Section 2.2 and Figure 3
evidence.detail: PCA shows fragmented V-JEPA 2 features. Authors hypothesize that visible tokens lack local supervision and aggregate global information.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 5–6, Figure 4 and architecture paragraph
evidence.detail: Image/video patch embeddings feed shared encoders; multi-level features are fused before prediction. Blue context and orange masked branches have target-side stop-gradient. The caption mentions masked predictions, while the diagram, Eq. (2) and p. 6 explicitly include context predictions.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 5 and 7, Eqs. (2)–(3), Table 2 and Section 2.3.1
evidence.detail: Visible-token L1 is scaled by λ divided by the square root of distance to the nearest masked token. Warmup is described over epochs 50–100. Weighted λ=0.5 with warmup gives 33.8 ADE20K and 62.5 SSv2; prose instead states 33.9 and 0.473 NYUv2.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 7–8, Section 2.3.2
evidence.detail: Three intermediate outputs plus final output are concatenated and MLP-fused; predictor outputs at all four levels receive context and prediction losses. The p. 8 prose says 72.0 SSv2 whereas Table 1 gives 72.1.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 6–7, Figure 5 and Table 1, cumulative rows
PDF pp. 8–9, Table 3 and Sections 2.3.3–2.3.5
evidence.detail: VisionMix163M replaces 1M ImageNet images with LVD-142M; video weights emphasize SSv2 and YT-1B. LVD sampling-weight cells are blank; separate modality batches contain 2304 images and 128 videos. Native 2D 16×16 and 3D 16×16×2 patchifiers avoid image temporal duplication. Scaling reaches 2B ViT-G.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 6 and 33, implementation details, Appendix A and Table 12
evidence.detail: 135k primary steps, 12k warmup, 12k cooldown; 4-fps videos change from 16 frames at 256 to 64 at 384, images from 256 to 512. Predictor: 24 blocks, width 384; EMA 0.99925; weight decay 0.04; ViT-G taps [12,24,36,48]; λ=0.5 video/0.7 image. Learning rates: 1e-4 to 5.25e-4, then cooldown 6e-4 to 1e-6. Pretraining hardware/runtime/software versions are not specified.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 9 and 34, Section 2.3.6, Section 3 opening and Appendix B
evidence.detail: Frozen teacher replaces EMA targets; new 12-block predictor matches teacher output dimensions; no deep self-supervision. Student EMA is used for final output, not the loss. Teachers match pre-/post-cooldown stages. Section 3 describes downstream use of a frozen encoder.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 9–10, Section 3.1 and Figure 6
evidence.detail: Ego4D STA v2 has 98,276 train and 47,395 validation examples. Outputs are box, noun, verb and contact time in last-observed-frame coordinates. Top-5 mAP All uses IoU >0.5 and 0.25-second timing tolerance with four discounted false positives. Main text: eight video frames over 0.5 seconds at 384 pixels plus a 1080-pixel image; four feature scales.

evidence.location: PDF p. 11, Table 4, mAP All and component columns
evidence.detail: ViT-G mAP All 7.71 versus V-JEPA 2 6.02, DINOv3 7B 5.68 and STAformer 5.67. ViT-G AP_b 50.7, AP_b+V 25.8, AP_b+δ 20.2, mAP_N+δ 12.8; nearby prose says 12.9 with inconsistent notation. Literature and common-protocol rows are separated.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 35–36, Appendix C.4
evidence.detail: Last-frame queries attend to video keys/values, followed by interpolation, image-feature fusion, a 2D convolution and five pyramid scales (1/4 through 1/64). RPN/RoI features predict noun, verb and positive contact time. Selected configuration: 16 frames at 2 fps, 384 pixels, learning rate 1.2e-4; multi-size image training. Other encoders use best respective configurations.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 12 and 36, Table 5, Section 3.2 and Appendix C.6
evidence.detail: Validation action mean-class Recall@5: V-JEPA 2 1B 39.7, V-JEPA 2.1 1B 38.4, 2B 40.8. Context: 32 frames at 8 fps and 384×384; evaluation anticipates one second ahead. Frozen encoder/predictor outputs feed three classifier queries. Appendix describes randomized training anticipation and focal loss.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 12–13, Section 3.3, Figure 8 and Table 6
evidence.detail: Separate 24-layer approximately 300M action-conditioned predictor learns from raw DROID with teacher-forcing and two-step rollout losses. Franka Panda visual-goal MPC uses CEM and one A100, averaging ten tasks per skill. Matched planner (800 samples, 10 iterations, horizon 1, 3 s) gives grasp 60% vs 70%; changed planner (300,15,8,14 s) gives 80%. All rows give 100% reach and 80% pick-and-place. Gripper failures are described qualitatively.

evidence.location: PDF p. 14, Section 3.4, Figure 9 and Table 7
evidence.detail: Conditional diffusion predicts clean latent features with DDIM; CEM uses 480 two-second candidates at 4 fps and translation/yaw actions. Eight denoising steps replace at least 128. ViT-G/NWM: Tartan ATE 5.687/5.831, mean ATE 2.990/3.032, time 10.6/103.2 s. ViT-G has worse Recon and Sacson ATE. Caption says finetuning and normalized Average Trajectory Error; prose uses Absolute Trajectory Error without a normalization formula.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 15–16, Table 8 and Section 3.5
evidence.detail: ViT-G NYUv2/KITTI RMSE 0.307/2.461; ADE20K/Cityscapes/VOC mIoU 47.9/73.5/85.0; DAVIS/YT-VOS J&F 69.0/72.7. V-JEPA 2: 0.642/4.650, 24.4/45.9/63.9, 52.5/53.7. DINOv3 7B: 0.309/2.346, 55.9/81.1/86.6, 71.1/74.1. Prose segmentation deltas do not all equal Table 8 subtraction.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 15 and 34, Section 3.5 and Appendices C.1–C.2
evidence.detail: Dense probes use frozen final-layer image-tokenizer features. Depth uses a linear head with learned BatchNorm; segmentation uses normalized features and AdamW. ADE20K/VOC use 512 pixels for patch size 16 versus 448 for size 14; Cityscapes uses 1024-pixel height. Default depth resolutions and benchmark split details are not fully enumerated.

evidence.location: PDF p. 16, Section 3.5 results
evidence.detail: Authors hypothesize that fewer highly cluttered VisionMix scenes explain weaker ADE20K and Cityscapes segmentation.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 16–18 and 34–35, Section 3.6, Figure 13 and Appendix C.3
evidence.detail: First-frame masks propagate through local cosine-similarity neighbors without learned parameters. DAVIS has 60 train/30 validation videos; YouTube-VOS training videos are divided 80/20. Appendix selects hyperparameters on DAVIS training; Section 3.6 describes searches on each training split before applying the DAVIS configuration. Final settings: 15 context frames, circle size 12, top-5, temperature 0.2, 480-pixel short side.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 18–19, Table 9 and Section 3.7
evidence.detail: Frozen attentive probes average multi-clip logits. ViT-G SSv2/Diving-48/K400/IN1K: 77.7/89.2/87.7/85.5; V-JEPA 2: 77.3/90.2/87.3/85.1. Table 9: SSv2 16×2×3, K400 16×8×3, Diving-48 32×4×3. Literature probe architectures can differ.

evidence.location: PDF p. 36, Appendix C.5
evidence.detail: Four probe blocks use 16 attention heads, with final query cross-attention. SSv2 text prints 64×2×3 but calls it a 16-frame clip. Diving-48 uses four encoder layers and 50 epochs; most tasks use 20 epochs and a best-of-20-head sweep.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 19–20, Table 10 and Section 3.8
evidence.detail: Same-filtered-data rows: average 57.8/57.9 and PerceptionTest validation 80.1/83.1 for V-JEPA 2/2.1. TemporalBench drops 32.3 to 28.5 and TOMATO 41.4 to 38.0. Alignment uses Llama 3.1 8B, removes 18% of PerceptionLM via filters/Qwen3VL judging, and adds longer-context alignment and PerceptionTest training. Filtering thresholds are not given. Older starred PerceptionTest scores are test scores; that server is inactive.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 20–22, Section 3.9 and Figures 14–15
evidence.detail: Image/video PCA feature comparisons select the RGB-component permutation for visual appeal. They visualize structure rather than measuring a calibrated semantic or physical state.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 20 and 23, Section 3.10 and Table 11
evidence.detail: Scratch/distilled ViT-L: SSv2 74.2/76.5, ADE20K 42.0/46.7. Table 11 gives teacher DAVIS 69.0, distilled ViT-L 68.7, distilled ViT-B 67.0; p. 20 incorrectly compares ViT-L to teacher 67.0.

evidence.location: PDF p. 24, Section 5
evidence.detail: Emphasis is on representation learning; further scaling and dense world-model development for robotics are proposed.

evidence.location: PDF p. 37, Table 13 and Appendix D.1
evidence.detail: Without/with deep supervision, last-layer versus four-layer ADE20K: 34.9/39.1 versus 42.0/43.9; NYU: 0.513/0.463 versus 0.381/0.370; Diving-48: 85.8/86.9 versus 87.2/88.1. Four-layer gains shrink but remain positive.

evidence.location: PDF p. 37, Table 14 and Appendix D.2
evidence.detail: Higher video cooldown resolution improves many scores but not all: ViT-G Diving-48 falls 89.5 to 89.2 and YT-VOS 72.7 to 72.6; ViT-g DAVIS falls 68.0 to 67.4. High-resolution tracking entries differ from Table 8; the prose claim of gains across all tasks is too broad.
